subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 9 of Year 4 Computing at Ehel Academy. This unit is called “Be a Code Cracker”, and it is all about keeping information safe. It is one of the most exciting units of the year, and — happily — it needs no computers at all. Everything is done with a pencil, paper and a bit of clever thinking. There are three big ideas, and they fit together like a story. First, why do we need secrets? Because so much information now travels over networks and the internet — and when a network breaks (a network failure), or a bad person tries to steal information, that information is in danger. Second, the way we protect it is encryption: we disguise a message so only a person with the secret key can understand it. The word cipher simply means a secret way of writing: to encrypt is to turn a normal message (plain text) into a scrambled one (ciphertext), and to decrypt is to turn it back. These are not made-up school codes — the Caesar cipher is over two thousand years old, used by the Roman leader Julius Caesar, and the Pigpen cipher has been used since the 1500s.

outcomes: Explain that a network failure is when a fault in hardware or software stops a network working properly.
Give examples of problems caused by a network failure in a hospital, a school, for the police, and in a shop or bank.
Explain that encryption disguises a message so that only someone with the secret key can understand it.
Use the words plain text (before) and ciphertext (after), and say where and why encryption is used.
Explain that a cipher is a secret way of writing, and that Caesar and Pigpen are substitution ciphers (one letter is swapped for something else).
Encrypt and decrypt a message using the Caesar cipher with a chosen key, and know what to do when a letter goes past Z (wrap around to A).
Encrypt and decrypt a message using the Pigpen cipher, reading the symbols from the grid.
Invent a simple cipher of their own and understand why the person receiving a message needs the key.

Before this unit (from the syllabus), children should already know some things you can do on a network and its advantages and disadvantages, know what a cipher is, and be able to use a simple code to write and decode a short message. A two-minute recap — "what is a network, and what do we use it for?" — is enough to begin.

concepts.title: Networks, and what happens when they fail
concepts.explanation: A network is a set of computers and devices joined together so they can share things — files, messages and the internet. A network failure is when a fault in the hardware (the machines or cables) or the software (the programs) stops the network working properly. When the network is down, people cannot share files, send emails, reach the internet, or get to the information stored on the network. Start with a hook that shows why secrets matter.

concepts.title: What is encryption, and why do we use it?
concepts.explanation: Encryption means disguising a message so that only certain people can understand it. It uses a key — the secret that explains how the message has been disguised. The normal message is called plain text; the disguised message is called ciphertext. A very important idea: encryption does not stop someone seeing the letters of a message — it stops them understanding it. Even if someone snatches it, they just see “KHOOR” and cannot understand it. Only Leo, who has the same key, can decrypt it back to “HELLO”.
concepts.example: Answer this in your own words, out loud or on paper: What is encryption, and why do we use it? Then check your answer against the explanation above.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you use “plain text”, “ciphertext” and “key” correctly? Can you give one reason encryption is important?

concepts.title: The Caesar cipher: writing secret messages
concepts.explanation:
The Caesar cipher is one of the oldest ways to encrypt. You shift every letter along the alphabet by the same number of places. That number is the key. Julius Caesar himself often used a key of 3. Because you swap each letter for another letter, it is called a substitution cipher.

The top row is the normal alphabet; the bottom row is the same alphabet shifted along by 3. To encrypt, find your letter on the top and write the letter underneath it. Give you the Caesar alphabet strip (below).
concepts.example: Find one real example of the Caesar cipher: writing secret messages around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you handle the wrap-around at the end of the alphabet? Can you use the strip to encrypt a word correctly with a key of 3?

concepts.title: Cracking the Caesar cipher: decrypting
concepts.explanation: To decrypt a Caesar message you do the opposite of encrypting: shift each letter the same number of places backwards. If the key was 3, move each letter 3 places back. On the alphabet strip, find the letter on the bottom row and read off the normal letter above it. With a key of 3, decrypt KHOOR back to HELLO (K to H, H to E, O to L, O to L, R to O). Then try a whole sentence from the textbook, corrected here so it is exactly right: decrypt VHH BRX WRQLJKW with a key of 3 to reveal SEE YOU TONIGHT. Cracking a real sentence together is a thrilling moment — you can shout out the words as they appear.
concepts.example: Find one real example of cracking the Caesar cipher: decrypting around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you understand that decrypting shifts the opposite way to encrypting? Can you check your answer makes a real word or sentence? Can you decrypt a Caesar message with a given key?

concepts.title: The Pigpen cipher, and invent your own
concepts.explanation:
The Pigpen cipher is another substitution cipher, but instead of swapping a letter for a letter, it swaps each letter for a symbol. The alphabet is written into two grids and two crosses, and each letter's symbol is the shape around it. It has been used since the 1500s.

The first grid and the first cross use plain shapes; the second grid and second cross add a dot inside each shape.
concepts.example: Find one real example of the Pigpen cipher, and invent your own around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you understand, from the no-key test, why the person receiving a message must have the key?

workedExamples.solution: FRIEND with a Caesar key of 3 = IULHQG (F to I, R to U, I to L, E to H, N to Q, D to G).

workedExamples.title: Worked example 6: Networks, and what happens when they fail

esafety.title: Keep personal information private
esafety.text: Your full name, address, school, phone number, birthday and passwords are personal information. Never type them into a game, an app or a website, and never send them to someone you only know online.

esafety.title: Check before you trust
esafety.text: Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. Check an important fact on a second, different website, and ask an adult you trust if you are not sure.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.

selfAssessment: I can explain that a network failure is when a fault in hardware or software stops a network working properly.
I can give examples of problems caused by a network failure in a hospital, a school, for the police, and in a shop or bank.
I can explain that encryption disguises a message so that only someone with the secret key can understand it.
I can use the words plain text (before) and ciphertext (after), and say where and why encryption is used.
I can explain that a cipher is a secret way of writing, and that Caesar and Pigpen are substitution ciphers (one letter is swapped for something else).
I can encrypt and decrypt a message using the Caesar cipher with a chosen key, and know what to do when a letter goes past Z (wrap around to A).
I can encrypt and decrypt a message using the Pigpen cipher, reading the symbols from the grid.
I can invent a simple cipher of their own and understand why the person receiving a message needs the key.

I can before this unit (from the syllabus), children should already know some things you can do on a network and its advantages and disadvantages, know what a cipher is, and be able to use a simple code to write and decode a short message. A two-minute recap — "what is a network, and what do we use it for?" — is enough to begin.
